messages.subject: Large Covariance Matrix
parts:
All,

I am working on a project where I have 5 correlated outcomes observed for units ( 5 organs), clustered inside of individuals. Sample size (number of  individuals) is very small N=4-6, depending on context.

I have several covariates (N=19) with which to predict outcomes, that are unique at the individual level. Outcomes vary in terms of their support. Some outcomes are Gaussian, some are binary categories.

So in total we have 5 outcome measures for  5 "organs", clustered into 5 individuals, and 19 covariates with measures unique only at the individual level (the highest level in this hierarchy).

Thus the basic model setup is as below in pseudo-code (note my poor use of  the letter l, which looks like the number 1):
G[l,n]~Normal(b[l,1] + b[l,2]*X[n], sdG)

H[l,n]~Normal(b[l,3] + b[l,4]*X[n], sdH)

Y[l,n]~Bernouli(inv_logit(b[l,3] + b[l,4]*X[n]))
...

Where:

b[l,1:N]~mvn(mu[1:N],Sigma[1:N,1:N])
 
all of the cholesky parametrization is done to optimize, and proper priors get declared, etc...

The above model works fine, and I can use WAIC to compare each predictor, by comparing each of the 19 bivariate models, and a null intercept only model.

I was recently pointed to Bayesian lasso procedures as an alternate analytic strategy where (in pseudo-stan code):
G[l,n]~Normal(X[n]*b[l,1:19], sdG)

H[l,n]~Normal(X[n]*b[l,20:38], sdH)

Y[l,n]~Bernouli(inv_logit(X[n]*b[l,39:50something]))
...

Where:
b[l]~mvn(mu,Sigma)

and mu has sharply regularizing double_exponential priors


This model wont run because Sigma is a large 95X95 matrix. The problem persists even
where:
Sigma <- diag_matrix(sigma) * cholesky_decompose(Rho);

In fact it is this line of code that throws the error:
  (Warmup)Error : error in call to cholesky decomposition; require symmetric matrix, but found; x[9,32]=0.0088246; x[32,9]=0.0088246

Since sample size is so small, and the outcomes variables are highly correlated measures of essentially the same empirical outcome,  I really like the idea of letting the regression parameters be drawn from a multivariate normal, rather than assuming that they are independent things.

Is it possible to get something like this running in Stan? I have seen threads on here about hand coding a hack to get around the computational burdens of such a big cov matrix, but they were used when the matrix was known data. Is there any similar strategies when the matrix is random?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Large Covariance Matrix
parts:
On Tuesday, March 18, 2014 11:05:40 PM UTC-4, Cody Ross wrote:
Ben,

I can't seem to understand what you are saying.

I use that line of code to do the operation:
L <- cholesky_decompose(  diag_matrix(sigma) * Rho* diag_matrix(sigma)   );

Oh...

I see... Sigma is not a covariance matrix, Sigma is a Cholesky factor. I just named it Sigma in my code since I'm using multi_normal_cholesky(mu, Sigma). My bad for not being more explicit about this.

Sigma is a correlation matrix, and thus has a Cholesky factor. But rather than declaring Sigma in the parameters block and subsequently calculating its Cholesky factorization (which is slow and prone to numerical errors that you ran into when the dimension is large), it is much better to declare the ingredients of its Cholesky factor in the parameters block, construct and use the Cholesky factor, and never actually form Sigma (unless you want to). Also, this can be combined with a multivariate Matt trick to avoid calling any of the multi_normal() functions.

Maybe the new attachment is clearer. Basically, you do a lot of convoluted stuff to construct L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix with an LKJ distribution. Then, you use the fact that if

b[l] <- mu + sigma .* (L * z[l]);

where z[l] has independent standard normal priors, then b[l] is has an implicit multivariate normal prior with mean vector mu and covariance matrix diag_matrix(sigma) * L * L' * diag_matrix(sigma), but you never actually form that covariance matrix.

Ben
